list.listitem: Reiters syndrome (reactive arthritis, ReA) is a clinical syndrome classified as a seronegative spondylarthropathy. C
Patients typically present with asymmetric oligoarthritis of lower extremities, enthesitis, conjunctivitis or anterior uveitis, and urethritis after a genitourinary infection or enteric infection. C

There is no single laboratory test for diagnosing ReA. Laboratory tests are used to confirm a preceding or ongoing enteric or genitourinary infection and to exclude other causes of mono- or oligoarticular arthritis. C
NSAIDS are the mainstay of symptomatic treatment for acute ReA, although data are lacking to show that NSAIDS shorten or otherwise alter the course of the disease. B

The prognosis is usually good. Most patients remit spontaneously within 3 to 12 months of onset of ReA; 10% to 15% of patients have chronic or relapsing arthritis and may develop ankylosing spondylitis. C

background.definition: ReA (formerly called Reiter's syndrome) is the triad of sterile inflammatory peripheral arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis that appears shortly after certain infections of the genitourinary or gastrointestinal tracts.

list.listitem: The annual incidence is 4.6/100,000/y for Chlamydia-induced arthritis and 5/100,000/y for enterobacteria-induced ReA.
The incidence does appear to be decreasing with improved food safety and better treatment of sexually transmitted infections.

ReA most frequently occurs in patients in their fourth or fifth decade of life, but it can occur at any age. The form of ReA that occurs after venereal infection occurs more frequently in males (ratio 9:1).
The form that develops after bowel infection (dysentery) occurs in equal frequency in males and females.
Infection: ReA can occur after venereal infections with Chlamydia trachomatis and GI infections with Yersinia, Salmonella, Campylobacter, or Shigella.

Genetic: ReA shares features with ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease-associated spondyloarthritis. These diseases are strongly linked to the genetic marker HLA-B27, have an absence of rheumatoid (Rh) factor, and frequently occur with extraarticular symptoms.

The HLA-B27 gene is commonly seen in patients with ReA. The presence of HLA-B27 may predict a more severe and prolonged form of the disease. Not all individuals with ReA have the HLA-B27 gene, suggesting that other genetic or environmental factors also play a role.

A survey of Canadian rheumatologists reported that many cases of ReA in their practices had an unknown cause, and that the overall rate appears to be declining, perhaps due to less foodborne illness and more prompt threatment of STIs.
It has been reported following use of intravesical BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guerin) therapy for bladder cancer, with a mean age of 61 years and occuring after a mean of 6 instillations.
Despite knowing the initiating event (infection) and genetic constitution (many patients have HLA-B27) of ReA, we do not yet understand the pathogenesis of this disorder.

Microbial antigens are present within the joints of patients with ReA. Chlamydia, Yersinia, Salmonella, and Shigella antigens have been detected in the synovial fluid or in synovial tissue and also in some asymptomatic controls.

The presence and persistence of microbial structures in the host is not well understood but could be explained by impaired elimination of the microbes from the joint by alterations of gene or protein expression in infected host cells, a poor T-helper (especially Th2) cytokine response or the defective function of HLA-B27.
ReA typically presents as an asymmetric oligoarthritis of lower extremities, enthesitis, conjunctivitis or anterior uveitis, and urethritis following a genitourinary infection or enteric infection. C

Perform basic blood work to rule out other rheumatologic causes: ReA typically presents with a mild normocytic normochromic anemia, leukocytosis (10,000-15,000/mm3), thrombocytosis (400,000-600,000/mm3), elevated ESR, negative Rh factor, and negative antinuclear antibody (ANA). B

Older men, podagra, severe, limited-duration attacks
Migratory polyarthritis, prompt response to salicylates

list.listitem: History and physical should focus on the following symptom clusters.

Arthritis: Reactive arthritis (ReA) usually occurs 2 to 4 weeks after a venereal infection or episode of gastroenteritis. The classic joints that can become inflamed in ReA are the knees, ankles, and feet. However, about 50% of patients have arthritis in the upper extremities, and some have polyarthritis in the small joints.
Enthesitis: pain, swelling, and tenderness most commonly at points of insertion of the Achilles tendon and plantar aponeurosis.
Sacroilitis: Low back and buttock pain occurs in approximately 50% of cases, 12% of patients will go on to develop ankylosing spondylitis.

Extraarticular signs and symptoms: include genitourinary tract symptoms and gastroenteritis; conjunctivitis/iritis usually develops within several days of urethritis and occurs in 20% of patients. Keratoderma blennorrhagica is waxy, papular pustules or psoriatic patches that can occur anywhere but most commonly on palms and soles. Cercinate balanitis is moist, shallow ulcers or dry, hyperkeratotic psoriatic-like lesions on shaft and glans of penis. Oral ulcers are shallow and usually painless. Nail changes include crumbling destruction but no pitting, resembling psoriatic arthritis. Aortitis is seen in rare individuals.

There is no agreement on how to diagnose ReA. Laboratory testing is used to confirm a preceding or ongoing enteric or genitourinary infection and to exclude other causes of mono- or oligoarticular arthritis.

Identifying the infectious cause: screening for C. trachomatis via urine/urethra/cervix samples is recommended and is usually sensitive. In the case of enterobacteria, stool cultures for a triggering pathogen are suggested. However, at the time of arthritis, the symptoms of triggering infection have usually passed and the stool cultures are usually negative.

Serology: serological testing is useful in GI infection-associated ReA. Serology is positive for infections in about 50% of patients diagnosed as having possible or probable ReA. However, there are no internationally validated standard serological techniques.

Basic blood work: ReA typically presents with a mild normocytic, normochromic anemia, leukocytosis (10,000-15,000/mm3), thrombocytosis (400,000-600,000/mm3), elevated ESR, negative Rh factor, and negative ANA.
Joint aspiration: examination of the synovial fluid for crystals, Gram stain, and culture should be done to exclude crystal-associated or septic arthritis.

HLA-B27 gene marker: not routinely evaluated. Typing for HLA-B27 is positive in 65% to 75% of white patients with ReA but is less common 30% to 50% in African Americans. HLA-B27 is more likely to be found in patients with a chronic relapsing and remitting course as well as those with sacroiliitis and aortitis.

Other tests: polymerase chain reaction and immunostaining have identified Chlamydia and enterobacteria antigens in synovial tissue. However, these tests have never been evaluated prospectively as diagnostic tools and are currently only used as research techniques.

Radiology: x-rays may reveal positive findings when arthritis persists for longer than 3 months. Typical changes include erosive bony changes and a fluffy periosteal reaction at tendon insertion points.
ReA is a clinical diagnosis and should be suspected in patients with the triad of symptoms arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis who have had a recent genitourinary or enteric infection.
Laboratory testing is used to confirm a preceding enteric or genitourinary infection via urethral or vaginal cultures and smears.
Blood work and joint aspiration are performed to exclude other causes of mono- or oligoarticular arthritis.

Treatment of ReA includes antibiotics for treatment of C. trachomatis (but not gastroenteritis), NSAIDS for pain control and rarely disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors for patients with persistent symptoms.
Treat acute C. trachomatis infections in patients and their partners (azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose or doxycycline 100 mg twice per day for 7 days). A
Antibiotic therapy is not indicated for uncomplicated enteric infections; it does not affect subsequent arthritis. A
NSAIDs can be useful for pain control but do not affect the course of illness. B

Antibiotics should be used to treat acute C. trachomatis infections in patients and their partners; this has been shown to decrease significantly the rates of ReA. Azithromycin (1 gm orally as a single dose) or doxycycline (100 mg twice per day for 7 days) should be used.

Antibiotic therapy is not indicated for uncomplicated enteric infections; it has not been shown to affect subsequent arthritis. Long-term antibiotic treatment has not been shown to reduce the length or severity of ReA.
There is no evidence that NSAIDs shorten or otherwise affect the course of the disease, but they can be useful for pain control.
Corticosteroid injections can be helpful for pain and swelling of arthritis and plantar fascitis.

Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs are indicated for patients with persistent symptoms (>3-6 months), erosive joint disease, or recurrent flares. Sulfasalazine is well tolerated and effective at a dose of 1 g twice or three times daily. A trial randomized 134 patients who did not respond to NSAIDs to sulfasalazine 2000 mg/day or placebo. At the end of the treatment period response rates were significantly higher for sulfasalazine (62% vs 48%, p = 0.02, NNT = 7) and were accompanied by larger reductions in inflammatory markers.
TNF inhibitors are usually not indicated, but small studies have suggested effectiveness.
A survey of Canadian rheumatologists found that they used NSAIDs, intra-articular steroid injections, and DMARDs, and for chronic ReA most used TNF alpha inhibitors.
Physical therapy modalities are an integral part of management of ankylosing spondylitis. The aims of physiotherapy are to improve mobility and strength and to prevent stiffness and deformities.
ReA usually runs a self-limited course of 3 to 12 months. B

Ten to twenty percent of patients may continue to have chronic and destructive and disabling arthritis or enthesitis 2 years after the onset of symptoms. Ten to fifteen percent may progress to ankylosing spondylitis. B
Mortality from ReA is not common and results from cardiac complications such as aortitis. B
